figures.caption: Figure 1: SnapLGR Training pipeline. Stage 1: Tokenization (§2.1). We train an RQ-VAE on multimodal Qwen3-VL embeddings with PPR-based co-engagement supervision to produce the video-to-SID map. Stage 2: CPT (§2.2.1). We ground newly added SID embeddings in the LLM’s vocabulary using video text descriptions. Stage 3: SFT (§2.2.2). We fine-tune the full LLM to predict future engaged SIDs from users’ SID interaction histories.
Figure 3: SID collision concentration. SIDs are ordered by decreasing bucket size. Lower curves indicate a more balanced assignment; dashed guides mark the largest 1% of SIDs and 50% video coverage.
Table 3: Offline SID retrieval performance comparison over Qwen3-VL SIDs. SnapLGR yields a greater than 2× improvement across all top-𝑘 metrics relative to the T5 baseline.
Table 9: Full performance comparison between the legacy T5 encoder-decoder baseline and the reference SnapLGR.
Table 10: Complete SID-level metric grid for the SID-type comparison of Table 5 (models trained with MM, MM+, and Qwen3-VL SIDs).
Table 11: SFT (SID-only, from random initialization) retrieval eval across downscaled Qwen3 sizes. Sizes are backbone (non-embedding) params.
Table 12: Effect of training data scale. Below gives metrics across checkpoints of an SFT-only (no CPT) training run. Columns give training progress as a fraction of one epoch.
Figure 6: Example SID-to-video mappings. Each row contains images from 10 randomly-selected videos with the same SID. Videos with the same SID are highly semanticallysimilar.
Table 13: Completemetrics for the initialization comparison of Table 4 with both runs SFT-only, no CPT. Deltas are pretrained relative to random-init.
Table 14: Effect of beam width on SID-level metrics for baseline SFT-only checkpoint.
